structure.title: Learning to feel inferior
structure.text: Pip's childhood joins affection, fear, and shame to his first encounters with wealth.

structure.title: Becoming a gentleman
structure.text: New opportunities test what Pip thinks money and social polish can repair. His adult narration keeps revisiting the younger self's assumptions.

people.name: Pip
people.text: An orphan boy raised by his sister and her blacksmith husband in the Kent marshes, who tells his own story as an older man looking back.

people.name: Joe Gargery
people.text: Pip's kind, unlettered brother-in-law, who loves him like a son and whose decency Pip learns to be ashamed of.

people.name: Estella and Miss Havisham
people.text: A rich, eccentric recluse who never leaves her decaying house, and the proud, beautiful girl she is raising, with whom Pip falls in love.

context.title: Gentility
context.text: Becoming a gentleman involves manners, income, and social recognition. Moral goodness and genteel appearance need not coincide.
context.takeaway: Ask what Pip means by improvement.

context.title: Retrospective narration
context.text: The older Pip can expose a mistake while recreating how convincing it once felt. Shame and sympathy coexist in the telling.
context.takeaway: Separate the child's judgment from the narrator's.

notice.text: Follow hands, clothing, and table manners.
notice.why: Bodily details become evidence in Pip's private ranking of people.
Loyalty can be easy to overlook when it offers no prestige.

opening: Pip is ashamed of the hands that raised him. A visit to a rich woman's decaying house has taught the blacksmith's boy that his clothes, speech, and family are embarrassments, and that a beautiful girl can make him feel grateful for her contempt. When money unexpectedly arrives, he thinks his real life can begin. Dickens follows the pleasures of becoming impressive alongside the small betrayals it requires, as Pip learns to mistake the people he wants to resemble for the people he should trust.
